f.title: Review all safety information but avoid duplicate reporting to FDA

FDA expects sponsors to review all information, but to avoid duplicate reporting to the agency.
f.clause: Preamble II.B Overview of the Final Rule - Review of Safety Information
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.
f.processes: Safety intake & collection; Case processing & follow-up

f.title: Use sponsor judgment to decide whether an adverse event is a suspected adverse reaction qualifying for expedited reporting
f.statement: The sponsor must continue to evaluate the evidence and use its judgment to determine whether an adverse event meets the definition of suspected adverse reaction and qualifies for expedited reporting under 21 CFR 312.32(c).

f.title: Report as life-threatening any event that either the sponsor or the investigator considers life-threatening
f.statement: Reasons for differences of opinion between sponsor and investigator need not be included in the IND safety report, but any adverse event or suspected adverse reaction considered life-threatening by either the sponsor or the investigator should be reported as such.

f.title: Sponsor (not investigator) generally determines expectedness for reporting
f.statement: Unless a sponsor-investigator is responsible for the clinical trial, the sponsor, rather than the investigator, generally determines whether a suspected adverse reaction is unexpected for reporting purposes; judgment is needed to decide whether severity is greater than described in the investigator brochure.
f.clause: Preamble III.A.6 Unexpected SADR, response to Comment 7
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

f.title: Do not add long lists of unlikely adverse events to the investigator brochure; use judgment on the threshold for adding events
f.statement: Sponsors should not add to the investigator brochure long lists of adverse events that are unlikely to have been caused by the drug, because such lists could dilute clinically meaningful risk information and put subjects at risk. The sponsor needs to exercise judgment on whether the threshold for adding a newly observed adverse event has been reached, usually depending on the strength of evidence from individual or multiple cases and previous knowledge of the drug or class; the threshold may be lower if the event could result in a significant adverse outcome for trial participants.
f.clause: Preamble III.A.6 Unexpected SADR, response to Comment 8
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: It is not appropriate for sponsors to add long lists of adverse events that are unlikely to have been caused by the drug to the investigator brochure because such lists could dilute the importance of clinically meaningful risk information and as a result, may put subjects at risk. The sponsor needs to exercise judgment when deciding if the threshold has been reached for adding a newly observed adverse event to the investigator brochure. This decision usually depends on the strength of the evidence from individual or multiple cases and previous knowledge about the drug or drug class. In some cases, the threshold for including an adverse event may be lower if it could result in a significant adverse outcome for trial participants.
rows.location: Preamble III.A.6 Unexpected SADR, response to Comment 8

f.title: Update the investigator brochure on an ongoing basis; report similar serious suspected adverse reactions expeditiously until it is updated
f.statement: FDA expects the sponsor to update the investigator brochure on an ongoing basis with new important safety information. Until the investigator brochure and other applicable reference safety information are updated to include a new serious suspected adverse reaction, subsequent reports of similar serious suspected adverse reactions must be submitted expeditiously in IND safety reports.

f.title: A DCSI may be incorporated into the investigator brochure as the expectedness reference
f.statement: FDA does not formally adopt the Developmental Core Safety Information (DCSI) document, but a sponsor could incorporate a document such as the DCSI into the investigator brochure as the reference for expectedness for reporting purposes, if the DCSI contains the required safety information about the investigational drug.

f.title: Treat listed safety information sources as examples; meetings can also yield reportable information
f.statement: The sources listed in 21 CFR 312.32(b) are not all-inclusive but examples; reportable information can come from other sources, such as public or private meetings.

f.title: Submit marketing-experience reports for US-marketed drugs under postmarketing requirements, not to the IND
f.statement: In general, an expedited report from domestic or foreign commercial marketing experience for a drug lawfully marketed in the United States would not be submitted to the IND, but must be submitted under the relevant postmarketing reporting requirements (e.g., 21 CFR 310.305, 314.80, 600.80). The same applies to a suspected adverse reaction from foreign marketing experience for a different formulation (same active moiety) of a drug lawfully marketed in the United States.
f.clause: Preamble III.B Review of Safety Information, response to Comment 10
f.applicability: Drugs lawfully marketed in the United States; Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

f.title: Consider in vitro microsusceptibility, drug interaction and genotoxicity data as potential safety information
f.statement: Data from in vitro microsusceptibility, drug interaction or genotoxicity studies are examples, besides carcinogenicity, mutagenicity and teratogenicity, of in vitro data that may yield important safety information for IND review.
f.clause: Preamble III.B Review of Safety Information, response to Comment 11

f.title: Start the IND safety report clock (day zero) when the sponsor determines the information qualifies; actively seek missing information
f.statement: The reporting clock starts (day zero) as soon as the sponsor determines that the information qualifies for reporting under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i)-(iv). For a serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction from a clinical trial, this is the day the sponsor receives the information from the clinical investigator. If any information needed to evaluate and report the suspected adverse reaction is missing or unknown, the sponsor should actively seek it.
f.clause: Preamble III.C IND Safety Reports (Requirement for Minimum Data Set), response to Comment 13
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.deadline: Day zero = day the sponsor determines the information qualifies for reporting; for a serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction from a clinical trial, the day the sponsor receives information from the clinical investigator

For a serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction from a clinical trial, this would be the day the sponsor receives information from the clinical investigator. f.title: Promptly and diligently attempt to obtain information needed to evaluate a suspected adverse reaction
f.statement: Because 21 CFR 312.32(d)(1) requires sponsors to promptly investigate all safety information received, sponsors are expected to promptly and diligently attempt to obtain the information needed to evaluate a suspected adverse reaction and to actively seek critical missing or unknown information. A chronological history of these efforts need not be included in the IND safety report, and the regulations do not prescribe specific due diligence procedures.
f.clause: Preamble III.C IND Safety Reports (Requirement for Minimum Data Set), response to Comment 14
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: Under Sec. 312.32(d)(1), sponsors are required to promptly investigate all safety information received, so it is inherent in that requirement that sponsors promptly and diligently attempt to obtain the information necessary for evaluating a suspected adverse reaction. If critical information is missing or unknown, the sponsor should actively seek the information. The regulations do not include specific procedures for conducting or documenting due diligence activities because the agency recognizes that there is more than one approach that would be appropriate, depending on the situation.
rows.location: Preamble III.C IND Safety Reports (Requirement for Minimum Data Set), response to Comment 14
rows.review_note: Review: no change. 2025 FDA IND safety guidance cross-check: not contradicted, but the guidance now recommends that sponsors maintain records of their efforts to obtain follow-up information (guidance row 0161), going beyond this preamble's statement that no specific documentation procedure is prescribed. f.title: Retain IND safety records for 2 years after approval or after investigational shipment is discontinued and FDA notified
f.statement: Sponsors are required under 21 CFR 312.57(c) to retain records and reports required under part 312, including safety information received, for 2 years after a marketing application is approved for the drug or, if no application is approved, until 2 years after shipment and delivery of the drug for investigational use is discontinued and FDA has been notified. FDA may audit these records during inspection.

f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.
f.processes: Data integrity & records; Audit & inspection readiness

f.title: Include all sponsor-held INDs and other relevant information in the analysis of similar reports
f.statement: FDA expects the analysis of the significance of the suspected adverse reaction in the context of similar reports to include all INDs held by the sponsor and any other relevant information of which the sponsor is aware.

f.title: Maintain processes to periodically review safety data and update the investigator brochure, including postmarketing study data
f.statement: Companies should have processes in place to periodically review and analyze their safety data and update their investigator brochures with significant new safety information. The analysis should evaluate the suspected adverse reaction in the context of other related reports or adverse events, including those that may have occurred in postmarketing studies.
f.clause: Preamble III.D Serious and Unexpected SADR, response to Comment 16
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

f.title: Send IND safety reports to investigators under all open INDs, including investigator-sponsored INDs
f.statement: The sponsor must report to participating investigators under all open INDs, including those held by the sponsor and those to which the sponsor provides the investigational drug (investigator-sponsored).

f.title: Send follow-up reports to investigators only when they significantly affect subject care or study conduct
f.statement: Follow-up reports should be sent to investigators when an important suspected adverse reaction significantly affects the care of subjects or the conduct of the study. Minor refinements that do not significantly affect subject care or study conduct need to be sent to FDA but need not be sent to investigators; such information may be communicated to investigators in a routine update of the investigator brochure.

f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

Minor refinements that do not significantly affect care of subjects or conduct of the study need to be sent to FDA but need not be sent to investigators. Such information may be communicated to investigators in a routine update of the investigator brochure.

f.title: Confirm the event is serious, unexpected and a suspected adverse reaction before submitting a 312.32(c)(1)(i) report
f.statement: Before submitting an IND safety report under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i), the sponsor must determine that the event (1) is serious, (2) is unexpected, and (3) meets the definition of suspected adverse reaction in 312.32(a), i.e., there is a reasonable possibility that the drug caused the event. This determination will always require judgment based on the best available information.
f.clause: Preamble III.D Serious and Unexpected SADR, response to Comment 18
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: Before submitting an IND safety report under Sec. 312.32(c)(1)(i), the sponsor must determine that the event: (1) Is serious, (2) is unexpected, and (3) meets the definition of ``suspected adverse reaction'' in Sec. 312.32(a) (i.e., that there is a ``reasonable possibility'' that the drug caused the event). These criteria have not changed from former Sec. 312.32(c)(1)(i)(A). Making this determination will always require judgment based on the best available information.

f.title: Identify at protocol development the anticipated serious adverse events to be monitored rather than reported individually
f.statement: FDA agrees that, at protocol development, the sponsor should identify the serious adverse events (known consequences of the disease or events otherwise common in the study population) that it plans not to report individually in an expedited manner but will monitor during the trial, and encourages this process. If an aggregate analysis indicates those events occur more frequently in the drug treatment group, the sponsor must then report that information in an IND safety report under 312.32(c)(1)(i). The protocol list should be limited to events that are common even in the absence of drug exposure.
f.clause: Preamble III.E Alternative Reporting Arrangements, response to Comment 20
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.
f.processes: Clinical safety monitoring; Signal detection; Reporting policy

rows.quote: The agency agrees with the comments recommending that at the time of protocol development the sponsor identify the serious adverse events (i.e., known consequences of the disease or those otherwise common in the study population) that it plans not to report individually in an expedited manner but that it will monitor during the course of the trial. FDA encourages use of this process. Should an aggregate analysis indicate that those events occur more frequently in the drug treatment group, the sponsor must then report that information in an IND safety report under Sec. 312.32(c)(1)(i). However, the agency recognizes that it is not possible, nor desirable, to list in the protocol every adverse event that may be anticipated to occur in the study population; the protocol should therefore limit such a list to those events that are common, even in the absence of drug exposure.

f.title: FDA may require alternative or continued expedited reporting; sponsors may request a different format or frequency
f.statement: Under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(3), FDA may require a sponsor to continue to report expeditiously a medically significant suspected adverse reaction that is listed in the investigator brochure as observed with the drug (i.e., expected) so that its rate can be carefully monitored, and may require an alternative reporting format or frequency once a study or design has been identified as posing a potential or unforeseen risk to participants. A sponsor may request that a certain adverse event be submitted in a different format or at a different frequency than required.

f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

In other instances, a sponsor may request that a certain adverse event be submitted in a different format or at a different frequency than required. Section 312.32(c)(3) permits such arrangements.

f.title: Break the blind for serious, unexpected suspected adverse reactions that must be reported expeditiously
f.statement: Because there should generally be no need to report study endpoints in an IND safety report, unblinding due to such endpoints should typically not occur. Where a serious, unexpected suspected adverse reaction must be reported expeditiously, FDA expects the blind to be broken.

f.title: Describe in the protocol any alternative arrangement to maintain the blind and discuss it with the FDA review division
f.statement: If patient safety can be assured without breaking the blind, FDA encourages the sponsor to discuss alternative reporting arrangements with the appropriate FDA review division. f.title: A data monitoring committee may periodically analyze aggregated unblinded events while investigators remain blinded
f.statement: Some sponsors have used a data monitoring committee (DMC) to monitor overall event rates as the safety database accumulates in ongoing studies. A DMC could periodically analyze and evaluate the aggregated, unblinded events in the entire IND safety database to determine whether the drug is the suspected cause, while investigators and study participants remain blinded.
f.clause: Preamble III.F Unblinding, response to Comment 22
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

A DMC could periodically analyze and evaluate the aggregated, unblinded events in the entire IND safety database to determine if the drug is the suspected cause. During these analyses, investigators and study participants would remain blinded.

f.statement: For reporting findings under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(ii), a significant risk in humans includes instances of significant impairment or dysfunction.

f.title: Do not report routine updates of the investigator brochure or informed consent in expedited IND safety reports
f.statement: Ordinarily, a finding is considered suggestive of a significant risk in humans if it results in a safety-related change in the protocol, informed consent, investigator brochure or other aspects of overall conduct of the clinical investigation. Nonurgent, routine updates to the investigator brochure and informed consent do not meet the reporting criteria and should not be reported in an expedited IND safety report.

f.clause: Preamble III.G, response to Comment 27
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: The requirement has been revised to make it clear that, ordinarily, a finding would be considered suggestive of a significant risk in humans if it results in a safety-related change in the protocol, informed consent, investigator brochure, or other aspects of the overall conduct of the clinical investigation. Nonurgent, routine updates to the investigator brochure and informed consent would not meet the criteria for reporting under this provision and should not be reported in an expedited IND safety report.

f.title: Determine whether an animal finding suggests significant human risk; replication is not required
f.statement: The sponsor must determine whether a finding suggests a significant risk in humans for it to be reportable. Carcinogenicity, mutagenicity and teratogenicity are examples; others (e.g., significant organ toxicity at or near expected human exposure) could also qualify. Animal findings do not necessarily need to be replicated to meet the criteria for expedited reporting (e.g., a long-term carcinogenicity study need not be replicated); the validity of the model is a factor in evaluating the strength of evidence.
f.topic: Findings from animal or in vitro testing
f.clause: Preamble III.G, response to Comment 27
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: The sponsor must determine whether a finding suggests a significant risk in humans in order for the finding to be reportable. Animal findings such as carcinogenicity, mutagenicity or teratogenicity are meant to be examples of the types of findings that could suggest a significant human risk, but there are others that could meet the criteria for reporting. For clarity, the agency added another example in Sec. 312.32(c)(1)(iii) (i.e., reports of significant organ toxicity at or near the expected human exposure). Findings from animal studies do not necessarily need to be replicated to meet the criteria for expedited reporting to FDA. For example, the agency would not expect a long-term carcinogenicity study to be replicated if findings from the original study suggested a significant risk to humans. The validity of the model would be a factor taken into account in evaluating the strength of the evidence of significant risk.
rows.location: Preamble III.G, response to Comment 27
rows.review_note: Review: no change. 2025 FDA IND safety guidance cross-check: consistent (guidance rows 0060, 0061). Double-check: Preamble interpretation (2010 final rule), not codified text; preamble 'must' recorded as Recommended; long interpretive passage. Below 90 for these reasons.

f.title: Report in vitro findings only when the sponsor determines they suggest significant risk in humans
f.statement: An in vitro or animal finding is reportable in an IND safety report if it suggests a significant risk in humans exposed to the drug; the sponsor would not report an in vitro finding in an expedited report unless it determined that the finding suggests a significant risk in humans.

rows.location: Preamble III.G, response to Comment 28

f.title: Start the 15-day clock for nonclinical findings when the sponsor determines significant human risk; no final study report needed
f.statement: The 15-day reporting clock for a nonclinical finding begins (day zero) on the day the sponsor determines that the finding suggests a significant risk in humans. In general, a final study report need not be completed before the sponsor can make this determination.

f.title: Use FDA Form 3500A or narrative for domestic reports; CIOMS I accepted only for foreign reports
f.statement: FDA permits IND safety reports on FDA Form 3500A or in narrative format for domestic suspected adverse reactions, and on FDA Form 3500A, in narrative format or on a CIOMS I form for foreign suspected adverse reactions. FDA declines to permit domestic suspected adverse reactions on the CIOMS I form.
f.clause: Preamble III.H Submission of Written Reports, response to Comment 30
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

FDA declines to permit submission of domestic suspected adverse reactions on the CIOMS I form

f.title: Submit to a US-marketed drug's IND only reports from studies under that IND; route all others under postmarketing rules
f.statement: For a drug marketed or approved in the United States, the only reports that must be submitted to an IND are those arising from a study conducted under the IND (at domestic or foreign sites). All other reports (e.g., marketing experience, studies not under an IND) must be reported under the relevant postmarketing safety reporting requirements.

f.applicability: Drugs marketed or approved in the United States; Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

f.title: Submit IND safety reports in the manner and to the FDA location identified in the regulations
f.statement: Until FDA develops a system to route and manage IND safety reports within the AERS database or another database, the sponsor must submit IND safety reports in the manner described in the regulations and to the appropriate FDA location identified in the regulations.

f.title: Judge 'clinically important' rate increases by population, nature and seriousness, and magnitude of increase
f.statement: Deciding whether an increase in the rate of a serious suspected adverse reaction over that listed in the protocol or investigator brochure is clinically important is a matter of judgment based on factors including the study population, the nature and seriousness of the reaction, and the magnitude of the observed increase in rate.
f.clause: Preamble III.M Annual Reports, response to Comment 32
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: Deciding if an increase in the rate of a serious suspected adverse reaction over that listed in the protocol or investigator brochure is ) ``clinically important'' is a matter of judgment based on a variety of factors including the study population, the nature and seriousness of the reaction, and the magnitude of the observed increase in rate.
rows.location: Preamble III.M Annual Reports, response to Comment 32

f.title: Routinely review incidence rates of all serious and nonserious adverse events across the clinical program
f.statement: Sponsors should routinely review incidence rates of all serious and nonserious adverse events within their clinical program. If a clinically important increase in a serious suspected adverse reaction is identified compared with the rate in the protocol or investigator brochure, the sponsor must report it to FDA expeditiously. Changes in incidence rates of the most frequent nonserious adverse events would be reported in the IND annual report.
f.clause: Preamble III.M Annual Reports, response to Comment 32
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: The agency also agrees with the comment that sponsors should routinely review incidence rates of all serious and nonserious adverse events within their clinical program and expects that this is current practice within the industry. If a clinically important increase in a serious suspected adverse reaction is identified when compared to the rate described in the protocol or investigator brochure, the sponsor must report it to FDA expeditiously. Changes in incidence rates for the most frequent nonserious adverse events would be reported in the IND annual report.
rows.location: Preamble III.M Annual Reports, response to Comment 32

f.title: Investigators should report serious adverse events to the sponsor without delay once occurrence is confirmed
f.statement: FDA expects the investigator to notify the sponsor immediately of serious adverse events. It may take a day to collect adequate information to confirm the event occurred, but as soon as the investigator has confirmed it, the investigator should report it to the sponsor without delay.
f.clause: Preamble III.N Investigator Reports, response to Comment 36
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

f.title: Report serious adverse events from IND-exempt BA/BE studies conducted in the US; foreign studies go in the ANDA
f.statement: Sponsors of human bioavailability or bioequivalence studies that are exempt from the IND requirements but conducted in the United States must report any serious adverse events from the study to FDA (Office of Generic Drugs in CDER) and to all participating investigators under 21 CFR 320.31(d)(3). These requirements do not apply to IND-exempt studies conducted outside the United States; however, adverse event reports from foreign clinical studies must be included in the ANDA submission (21 CFR 314.94(a)(7)).
f.clause: Preamble III.O Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Requirements, response to Comment 37
f.applicability: IND-exempt human BA/BE studies; Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.
f.exceptions: Not applicable to IND-exempt BA/BE studies conducted outside the United States (their adverse event reports go in the ANDA)

rows.quote: Under Sec. 320.31(d)(3), sponsors of human bioequivalence or bioavailability studies that are exempt from the IND requirements under part 312, but are conducted in the United States, must report any serious adverse events from the study to FDA (to the Office of Generic Drugs in CDER) and to all participating investigators. These requirements do not apply to human bioavailability and bioequivalence studies that are exempt from the IND requirements under part 312 and are conducted outside of the United States. However, as part of the information required to establish that the proposed drug product can be expected to have the same therapeutic effect as the reference listed product, adverse event reports that occurred in foreign clinical studies must be included in the ANDA submission (see Sec. 314.94(a)(7)).
rows.location: Preamble III.O Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Requirements, response to Comment 37

f.title: Notify investigators of serious, unexpected suspected adverse reactions in studies of marketed products regardless of indication
f.statement: FDA rejected limiting investigator notification for investigations of marketed products to studies in a patient population or indication different from that approved. Regardless of the patient population or indication, information about a serious, unexpected suspected adverse reaction may influence the investigator's management of a trial participant and is therefore critical information for the investigator to receive; the sponsor's notification of participating investigators applies to such investigations.
f.clause: Preamble III.P Reports to Investigators and IRBs, response to Comment 38
f.applicability: Investigations of marketed products; Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: FDA does not agree with the comment that suggested that investigators not be notified of serious, unexpected suspected adverse reactions from investigations of marketed products unless the investigation is for a patient population or indication different from that approved. Regardless of the patient population or indication, information about a serious, unexpected suspected adverse reaction may influence the investigator's management of a clinical trial participant and, is therefore, critical information for the investigator to receive.

Double-check: Preamble interpretation (2010 final rule), not codified text; FDA's rejection of a comment; the sponsor duty is inferred from 312.32(c)(1). Below 90 for these reasons.

f.title: Apply 312.32 safety reporting to investigator-initiated (sponsor-investigator) studies
f.statement: FDA considers investigator-initiated studies synonymous with studies conducted by a sponsor-investigator (21 CFR 312.3), who is subject to both investigator and sponsor requirements; the safety reporting requirements under 21 CFR 312.32 therefore apply to an investigator-initiated study.
f.clause: Preamble III.Q Miscellaneous Comments, response to Comment 40
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: The agency considers investigator-initiated studies to be synonymous with studies conducted by a sponsor-investigator. A sponsor-investigator, as defined in Sec. 312.3, is ``an individual who both initiates and conducts an investigation, and under whose immediate direction the investigational drug is administered or dispensed. The term does not include any person other than an individual. The requirements applicable to a sponsor-investigator under this part [312] include both those applicable to an investigator and a sponsor.'' Therefore, the safety reporting requirements under Sec. 312.32 would apply to an investigator-initiated study.
rows.location: Preamble III.Q Miscellaneous Comments, response to Comment 40
rows.review_note: Review: no change. 2025 FDA IND safety guidance cross-check: consistent (guidance row 0025). Double-check: Preamble interpretation (2010 final rule), not codified text; interpretive scope statement. Below 90 for these reasons.

f.title: Classify as life-threatening if either investigator or sponsor views the event as placing the subject at immediate risk of death
f.statement: An adverse event or suspected adverse reaction is life-threatening if, in the view of either the investigator or the sponsor, its occurrence places the patient or subject at immediate risk of death. It does not include an event that, had it occurred in a more severe form, might have caused death.

f.title: Classify as serious if either investigator or sponsor views the event as resulting in a serious outcome

f.title: Consider important medical events serious when they may require intervention to prevent a serious outcome
f.statement: Important medical events that may not result in death, be life-threatening, or require hospitalization may be considered serious when, based upon appropriate medical judgment, they may jeopardize the patient or subject and may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed in the definition of serious. Examples include allergic bronchospasm requiring intensive treatment in an emergency room or at home, blood dyscrasias or convulsions that do not result in inpatient hospitalization, or the development of drug dependency or drug abuse.

f.title: Treat an adverse event as a suspected adverse reaction when there is evidence suggesting a causal relationship
f.statement: Suspected adverse reaction means any adverse event for which there is a reasonable possibility that the drug caused it. For IND safety reporting, reasonable possibility means there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the adverse event. Suspected adverse reaction implies less certainty about causality than adverse reaction, which means any adverse event caused by a drug.

For the purposes of IND safety reporting, ``reasonable possibility'' means there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the adverse event. Suspected adverse reaction implies a lesser degree of certainty about causality than adverse reaction, which means any adverse event caused by a drug.

f.title: Assess expectedness against the investigator brochure (or application risk information), including specificity and severity
f.statement: An adverse event or suspected adverse reaction is unexpected if it is not listed in the investigator brochure or not listed at the specificity or severity observed; or, if an investigator brochure is not required or available, it is not consistent with the risk information in the general investigational plan or elsewhere in the current application, as amended. For example, hepatic necrosis is unexpected (greater severity) if the brochure lists only elevated hepatic enzymes or hepatitis; cerebral thromboembolism and cerebral vasculitis are unexpected (greater specificity) if it lists only cerebral vascular accidents.
f.clause: 21 CFR 312.32(a) Definitions - Unexpected adverse event or unexpected suspected adverse reaction
f.applicability: Text as published in the 2010 final rule; later amendments are not in the captured text.

rows.quote: Unexpected adverse event or unexpected suspected adverse reaction. An adverse event or suspected adverse reaction is considered ``unexpected'' if it is not listed in the investigator brochure or is not listed at the specificity or severity that has been observed; or, if an investigator brochure is not required or available, is not consistent with the risk information described in the general investigational plan or elsewhere in the current application, as amended. For example, under this definition, hepatic necrosis would be unexpected (by virtue of greater severity) if the investigator brochure referred only to elevated hepatic enzymes or hepatitis. Similarly, cerebral thromboembolism and cerebral vasculitis would be unexpected (by virtue of greater specificity) if the investigator brochure listed only cerebral vascular accidents.
rows.location: 21 CFR 312.32(a) Definitions - Unexpected adverse event or unexpected suspected adverse reaction
